title: Slide a box up to the table's far edge without overhang
instruction: Slide the cardboard box as close as you can to the far edge of the table without letting any part of it hang over the edge.
context: Pushing an item flush with a counter, shelf or pallet edge, without overhang, is everyday work (e.g., for a household robot doing organization). Like many real life objects, the box is too large to grip, so the robot must push it with both arms. Near the edge, the box hides the gap from all of the robot's cameras, so it must estimate the gap from the box's size and position. The score increases with each centimetre, but any overhang gives 0, so the robot must decide how much risk to take given its imperfect estimate.
setup: Using yam_arena's 'station' setup. One object: a cardboard box, 50 cm deep, 40 cm wide and 20 cm tall with weight 1 kg, lying flat and square to the table in the middle of the table, centred between the arms. Its centre is 40 cm in front of the arm bases, so its back face is 15 cm in front of them and its front face is 26 cm from the table's far edge. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Measured once the episode ends. Score 0 if any part of the box hangs over any edge of the table (easily checked visually in real life), if the box is no longer flat on the table (numerically defined as tilt more than 10 degrees or lifted more than 1 cm, but easily checkable in real life), or if it is off the table. Otherwise, measure the gap: the perpendicular distance from the table's far edge to each of the two box corners nearest it, averaged. The score goes up linearly from 0 where the box started to 1.0 at a gap of 1 cm or less: (start gap - gap) / (start gap - 1 cm), kept between 0 and 1. The box need not start at exactly 26 cm, but our trials do (no random offset, for simplicity), so the score is (26 cm - gap) / 25 cm: 0.04 for each centimetre, for example 0.6 at a gap of 11 cm.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Put the box back in its starting position; a box that fell off the table is empty and light and can be picked up and replaced.
fidelity: Approximate: the box is a solid rigid block of uniform density, not a hollow box with flexible walls. Contact friction is rubber-like (static 1.2, dynamic 1.0), higher than cardboard on wood, so in simulation the box slides less after a push than a real one would. The table edge is perfectly sharp and the box does not deform or catch on it.
